review_text:
Honest and unbiased review!

Good game… for a new audience. It no longer feels like you're playing a traditional GTA game.

What made GTA stand out was its dark humor, its unfiltered portrayal of the world, and the freedom it gave players to make their own decisions, right or wrong. With this one, you can feel a shift in its culture, its target audience, and the way it portrays the world.

When you start GTA 5, you immediately get a sense of what LA is like: a shiny, materialistic world, shown to us through a middle-aged man going through a midlife crisis. It's a world full of chaos, where actions have few consequences and three men get away with almost anything. That's the foundation the game was built on, and it resonated with its target audience, which was mostly men.

This game starts you off as a tall, handsome military man and a woman who takes on the role men traditionally played in previous games. It's no longer built around what the original audience could resonate with. That's not a bad thing, though. The target audience is simply no longer just men.

GTA also used to go against the norms. It challenged mainstream narratives and never shied away from going after any group in society, exposing hypocrisy and attacking ideas the public held dear. This game feels much more timid. It takes the safer route so that as few people as possible are offended and as many as possible can relate.

That's what I mean by a cultural shift, and there's nothing wrong with it. The shift opens the game up to new audiences: people who are more sensitive to dark humor, or women who want to feel empowered by playing as a strong female protagonist. It's just not… GTA anymore, in the traditional sense of what GTA was. It feels like a corporate game that's trying to follow social guidelines. Still, it's very well made and the visuals are beautiful.

As for the mechanics, why change something that works? Running and driving were things people loved in the last two games, and they didn't need much change.

Characters in this one feel... boring, except Lucia. In the older GTA, all three characters were very different, and they all stood out with strong storylines and personalities. In this one, only Lucia stands out, which definitely makes me prefer to have her as the only playable character, unless more substance was given to the other protagonist. I also really love the addition of a female character, as it invites more women to this franchise.

Overall, it's a great game. It's just not like other GTA games, and it's definitely not a 10/10. It’s sad to see people rating it zero though because it is not fair either. I personally liked the older ones better for their storylines and gameplay, but this is not a bad game at all and is still worth playing. if this was not Rockstar and I was not comparing it to the older GTA games, I would give 8 or 9, but expectation is much higher for a company this reputable, so I will go with 7.
review_notes: Balanced pros/cons; explicitly explains 7/10 rating

review_text:
Gorgeous world, shameless business model. 6/10.
Visually, Leonida is a triumph of modern computer graphics—an $80–$100 interactive postcard with breathtaking dynamic lighting and world density. Unfortunately, once you stop admiring the sunsets and try to play it as a video game, the "100/10" hype shield evaporates fast:
1. Rent-Seeking in Offline Single-Player
Nothing screams "generational masterpiece" quite like opening the pause menu of an offline, full-priced single-player game and getting pitched a $7.99/month GTA+ subscription. Paying monthly rent for 10% shop discounts, free bus fare, a car model, and an early-game Crosstown garage—in a neighborhood the story actually moves you out of right after the first heist—is peak Take-Two "innovation." Back in 2004, San Andreas gave us cheat codes for free; in 2026, Rockstar sells them back as a recurring utility bill.
2. High-Definition Set Dressing Over Actual Gameplay
In a game set in South Florida, Rockstar built gorgeous, detailed tennis courts across the map solely as non-interactive background props—apparently full matches were too ambitious compared to 2013's GTA V. Instead, players are treated to tourist-trap mini-golf, shooting hoops alone, watching nonsensical TV cartoons, playing completely made-up fake games, and literally doomscrolling a fake social media feed on an in-game phone. Truly next-gen immersion.
3. 2013 Mission Rails at a Cinematic 30fps
That's 30fps on a good day—from time to time, even on PS5 Pro, you get scenes turning into a 20fps slideshow. And don't even get me started on the bugs and glitches I personally ran into throughout the campaign (no story spoilers here). Either way, a 30fps cap with noticeable stutters in 2026 already feels dated, especially paired with a 25-hour slow-burn intro and rigid mission scripts that fail you the second you step three feet off the developer's invisible railroad tracks.
4. Predatory One-Way Account Lock-In
No physical disc in the retail box, no cross-save progression, and zero cross-platform ownership—even though you are forced to link a Rockstar account. That account exists purely to serve you subscription ads, ensuring you get the privilege of buying the exact same game a second and third time when PC and next-gen ports will finally arrive.
Strip away the access-media paid applause, and you are left with a stunning diorama wrapped in cynical corporate extraction. Calling this a 6/10 is actually being very generous, I think—and I really mean it.
review_notes: Praises visuals briefly then tears down monetization, gameplay, 30fps, and lock-in

The writing and characters are the biggest letdowns. Jason is terribly written; he barely speaks, has zero agency, and never once questions or pushes back against Lucia’s catastrophic decisions, even though he’s the one paying the price and dealing with the fallout ruining their lives. As for Lucia, her character just doesn't work. The dialogue is weak, the story is below average, and the gameplay suffers from heavy repetition and boredom.
The only redeeming quality is the visuals—the graphics, attention to detail, and animations are great. However, that’s nothing miraculous; plenty of other games have achieved this level of visual polish while actually delivering where it counts.
It’s truly a shame, because the core pillars that make a game great—story, characters, and engaging missions—are completely missing here. Any review giving this game more than a 6/10 simply shouldn't be taken seriously.

review_text: I can’t say enough great things about this game. Though it’s not perfect as critics have let on, it is no where near as bad as these guys on the user reviews have made it out to be. What you’re given here is a true open world experience within the confines of the story they want to tell. This is very much Red Dead Redemption 2’s camp-to-camp style story, where you will travel from place to place to experience a little bit of everything this world has to offer. Zoos, parks, gyms, beaches, and just so much more come to mind when thinking about the vastness of what I’ve sunk about 45 hours into so far. Elements from every Rockstar game leading up to this point like bullet markers when shooting NPCs showing both where you hit and also how critical of a hit it was felt like it came straight from Max Payne 3. Choice option prompts to dice up small elements within interactions and missions take inspiration from LA Noire. Vehicle customization and races feel so much more fleshed out and along the lines of Midnight Club in this entry as opposed to those from the previous games. It draws heavy elements of gameplay and progression from both Red Dead and GTA as a whole. This is a very different breed of game and it has been controversial to say the least, but I couldn’t be happier. I have not been this immersed in a world since 2015’s The Witcher 3, and I believe this game will continue to push Rockstar’s creative ideas forward in the future. Easy 9/10 from me and I’m looking forward to seeing what comes next.
review_notes: Strong praise, easy 9/10
